paras: The Kansas City Southern train riot was an attack by a crowd of intoxicated white men on the coach for Black passengers of an incoming Kansas City Southern train bound for Lake Charles, Louisiana, on the night of February 22, 1903. According to the Associated Press dispatch, a Black passenger was shot to death and three white men were seriously injured, one of them probably fatally. The dispatch ran in white newspapers from Georgia to North Dakota, several times under headlines that named the white men as the aggressors.

The train carried a smoker, a ladies' coach and a sleeper as well as a separate car for Black passengers, called the "negro coach" in the dispatch and the "Jim Crow" coach in the New-York Tribune's headline. The men boarded at an unnamed sawmill town south of Leesville.

Once the crowd was aboard, "pandemonium began to reign," in the words of the dispatch as the Birmingham Age-Herald printed it. Trainmen kept the men out of the ladies' coach and the sleeper, according to the version in the Daily Ardmoreite, but the men took forcible possession of the smoker and then invaded the negro coach. A fight began at once; passengers reported shots and curses heard above the roar of the train, and the coach was almost wrecked, with all of its window lights knocked out.

A Black man was shot to death, and three white men were seriously injured, one of whom was expected to die of what was believed to be a fractured skull. The dispatch did not say who fired the fatal shot, and it gave no names. When the train reached DeQuincy, the trainmen put six of "the worst disturbers" off the train.

No arrests had been made when the report was sent, though officers were said to be "on the track of the marauders." No later report naming the dead man or recording an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press dispatch, datelined Lake Charles, February 23, appeared on February 24 in the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Richmond Times Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News, the St. Louis Republic, the New-York Tribune, the Wheeling Register and Delaware's Evening Journal. Over the next two days it reached the Bismarck Daily Tribune, the Daily Ardmoreite and the Williston Graphic.

Most papers headlined it simply as a riot on a train, but several placed the blame on the white men: the Age-Herald's headline read "White Ruffians Terrorize Train," the Savannah Morning News said the "Fatal Row Was Started by White Passengers," and the New-York Tribune announced a "Race Riot on Train" in which "White Men Invade 'Jim Crow' Coach." The dispatch itself called the attackers "ruffians" and "marauders," while some versions softened their drunkenness to "said to have been intoxicated." Other headlines put the Black victim first, as in the Montgomery Advertiser's "Negro Shot to Death and Three White Men Wounded," or presented a two-sided fight, as in the Williston Graphic's "Intoxicated White Men Get Into a Fight With Negroes." The Brandon News in Mississippi reduced the story to one line about a "free-for-all" riot near Lake Charles.

Weekly news digests carried a compressed version that changed the casualty count. The Evening Times-Republican of Marshalltown, Iowa, on February 26 and the Emmons County Record in North Dakota on March 13 said drunken white men "started a riot in the negro car" in which one colored man and three white men were seriously injured, "one fatally," without saying which man died. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press, and the white reports carried no account from the Black passengers themselves.

The dispatch reported a Black man shot to death and three white men seriously injured, while the New-York Tribune's headline spoke of "Two Whites Shot" above a text that gave three. The later digests counted one colored man among the seriously injured rather than the dead; because they condensed the earlier wire report, the dispatch's account of a Black man killed is the closer source. Most versions placed the riot on the night before a February 23 dateline; the Evening Journal said "Sunday night" (February 22), the St. Louis Republic "to-night."

bases: A crowd of white men forced its way into the coach for Black passengers and a Black man was shot to death in the ensuing fight, an assault on passengers rather than a hunt for an accused person (A1, A3, A10).
Every report descends from one Associated Press dispatch from Lake Charles (A1, A5); the digests (A12, A13, A14) condense it, and no independent local or follow-up account was found.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Lake Charles (passengers' report)
accounts.gist: Intoxicated white men boarded south of Leesville, seized the smoker, invaded the negro coach and started a fight in which a Black man was shot dead and three white men seriously hurt; six were put off at DeQuincy, no arrests.

accounts.label: Weekly news digests
accounts.gist: Drunken white men started a riot in the negro car in which one colored man and three white men were seriously injured, one fatally, without saying who died.

framing.detail: The Birmingham Age-Herald headlined 'White Ruffians Terrorize Train' and printed the dispatch's 'ruffians' and 'marauders'.
Most papers ran the AP text under 'Riot on a Train' headlines; Savannah's said the 'Fatal Row Was Started by White Passengers', New York's called it a 'Race Riot'.
The Williston Graphic's headline made it a fight between white men and 'Negroes', and the Brandon News called it a 'free-for-all' riot.

versions.value: A Black man shot to death

conflicts.note: The digests condense the earlier dispatch; the dispatch is the better evidence.
The Tribune's headline and its own text disagree; the text matches every other version.
Most versions point to the night of Feb. 22; later datelines (Feb. 24, 25) on reprints are re-dated copies.
